analysis.one_liner: Puts health warnings on sugary, ultra-processed foods and bans junk food ads aimed at children.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate health committee without a single cosponsor in July 2026 and now sits on the Senate calendar awaiting a floor vote that has not been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force front-of-package warning labels on sugary drinks, diet drinks, ultra-processed foods, and foods high in sugar, saturated fat, or sodium. It would make it illegal to market or advertise those products to children under 13 and restore the Federal Trade Commission's authority, curtailed since 1980, to write rules on children's advertising. It would also expand NIH research on nutrition and fund a public education campaign about diet and exercise.
analysis.who_benefits: Families and children benefit most: shoppers would see plain-language health warnings on the front of sugary and ultra-processed products, and companies could no longer target advertising at children under 13 using cartoons, influencers, toys, or kid-heavy media. The bill also funds NIH research on the health effects of ultra-processed foods and a CDC-run public education campaign, and it would lift a 1980 restriction that has stopped the FTC from regulating children's advertising. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Requires prominent front-of-package warnings on sugar-sweetened beverages, foods containing artificial or non-sugar sweeteners, ultra-processed foods, and foods high in nutrients of concern such as added sugar, saturated fat, or sodium; warnings for sweetened products must specifically say 'Not recommended for children.' [S2] [S3]

Makes it unlawful to market or advertise these 'junk food' products to children under 13, covering cartoons, influencers, toys and games, and any media where children are at least 30% of the audience; violations are treated as unfair or deceptive practices the FTC can penalize. [S2] [S3]
Repeals the 1980 provision that has blocked the FTC from issuing rules on children's advertising, restoring its ability to regulate ads aimed at kids. [S2] [S3]

Expands NIH nutrition research — including on ultra-processed foods, self-affirmed 'generally recognized as safe' additives, and how foods are engineered to be hyper-palatable — and directs a CDC public education campaign on nutrition, labels, and physical activity. [S2] [S3]

Exempts infant formula, medical beverages, meal replacements, milk, 100% juice, and alcohol from the sugar-sweetened beverage warning, so the mandate targets soft drinks and sports drinks rather than staple foods. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Food and beverage manufacturers bear the main cost: repackaging products to fit mandatory warning labels, reformulating to avoid warnings, and abandoning child-directed marketing. Advertising agencies and the media that sell children's advertising lose that revenue. Retailers and online sellers face labeling compliance, and those business costs would likely be passed to consumers at least partly. Federal agencies receive new funding to write and enforce the rules. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Food and beverage makers and advertisers

drawbacks.text: The definitions are broad: any food containing an emulsifier, stabilizer, flavoring, or similar industrial ingredient counts as 'ultra-processed,' so many ordinary grocery items — breads, yogurts, sauces — could carry a warning that consuming them 'can cause weight gain' and raise diabetes risk, even when eaten in normal amounts. [S3]

Diet drinks sweetened with stevia, aspartame, or sucralose would carry a bold 'Not recommended for children' warning even though they contain no sugar, sweeping in products many parents consider a better choice than soda. [S3]

Repackaging, reformulation, and compliance costs fall on manufacturers and retailers, and some of those costs would likely be passed on to consumers in prices; the committee version leaves the funding for FDA enforcement as unspecified 'such sums as may be necessary' rather than a firm amount. [S3]

Mandating specific government warning statements on lawful products invites First Amendment challenges over compelled commercial speech, and a ban on advertising judged 'child-directed' under a totality-of-the-circumstances test gives regulators substantial discretion over what companies may say — discretion that cuts both ways. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Front-of-package warning labels are one of the cheapest tools available: they change what is already on the shelf rather than banning products, and warning-label systems adopted by other countries have shifted purchasing toward less sugary items. The main honest criticism is scope — the 'ultra-processed' and 'high-intensity sweetener' definitions are wide enough to flag many everyday foods and all diet drinks, which could dilute the warning's meaning and impose real compliance costs. On balance the health benefit to families outweighs the cost to industry, but the bill would be stronger with tighter definitions.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health committee approved the bill in late July 2026 and placed it on the Senate calendar, where it waits for a floor vote no one has scheduled with barely five months left in the Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on July 16, 2026, and it was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee. He listed no cosponsors. [S1] [S4] [S5]

On July 22 the committee voted to report the bill favorably, and on July 28 it was reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute — meaning the committee replaced the original text with a rewritten version — and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 531. [S2] [S5]

The substitute softened several provisions from Sanders's original: rules for labeling food sold by online retailers are now discretionary, NIH research directives are prefaced with 'as appropriate,' the original's ban on meeting speakers financially affiliated with ultra-processed food manufacturers was removed, and specific authorizations ($60 million a year for NIH research, $10 million for the education campaign, $5 million for enforcement) were replaced with 'such sums as may be necessary.' [S3]
As of the latest record, no floor vote has been scheduled, and the 119th Congress ends January 3, 2027. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, food and beverage manufacturers and their advertisers: no labels have changed and no ad rules have taken effect. Families with children gain nothing unless the Senate actually takes up the bill before the Congress ends.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food and beverage makers, so far

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only cosponsor; his original draft set the mandatory warning labels, the children's advertising ban, and fixed funding amounts.

for.name: Bill Cassidy
for.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill through committee: it was ordered reported favorably on July 22 and reported by him with a substitute amendment on July 28, placing it on the Senate calendar.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has been held yet: the only sponsor is an Independent with zero cosponsors, yet the Republican committee chair reported the bill to the Senate calendar, so the partisan shape of a floor fight is unknown.

industries.industry: Food and beverage manufacturers (soda, snacks, ultra-processed foods)
industries.note: The bill's core target: makers of sugary drinks, diet drinks, and ultra-processed foods would have to print prominent government warnings on the front of their packages or reformulate, and their ability to sell to children through cartoons, influencers, and toys would be shut off. The bill's whole design is to move their customers — including children — away from these products.

Child-directed advertising for labeled junk food becomes unlawful, covering traditional media, social media, influencers, and in-game ads, and advertisers must include the warning labels in any remaining ads. It also revives the FTC's dormant power to write binding children's advertising rules, which the industry helped shut down in 1980.

industries.industry: Media platforms and networks with large child audiences
industries.note: Any media where children are at least 30% of the audience — from children's TV to YouTube channels, video games, and company websites — could no longer run ads for covered junk food, cutting a revenue stream.

Retailers must carry properly labeled products and the original draft required FDA to extend labeling rules to online sales; the committee version makes those online rules discretionary. The cost is real but modest compliance burden, not a change to what they can sell.

analysis.trajectory: Bills reported to the Senate calendar in late July, with no cosponsors and a crowded end-of-year agenda, rarely reach the floor before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027. The committee's favorable report by the Republican chair gives it a path, but unless Senate leadership schedules time or the bill is folded into a broader package, it will most likely die on the calendar when the Congress adjourns.
